overview.text: Gold occurs in lode systems including porphyry, vein and skarn deposits, as well as placers; these require different research and recovery methods.

researchNotes.title: Rocks & minerals
researchNotes.text: Gold is associated with copper-bearing porphyry systems and several vein and sulphide deposit types; a geological association does not establish recoverable stream gold.

researchNotes.title: Discovery & mining history
researchNotes.text: Historic camps include Cariboo–Barkerville, Bridge River, Rossland and Hedley. Their mining history is not evidence of open recreational access.

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: Approximate historical lode gold production: 32,000,000 ounces; 1858–2013. Approximate brochure total; do not combine with annual figures.

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: Approximate historical placer gold production: 6,000,000 ounces; 1858–2013. Separate from lode output; not a current reserve estimate.

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: Annual mine gold production: 17.6 tonnes; 2024. Preliminary; includes industrial production, not recreational returns.

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: Limited recreational hand panning uses a pan and hand shovel, without a Free Miner Certificate. Sluices, dredges and metal detectors are outside this permission. Obtain titleholder and private-owner consent where required; parks and other excluded lands are not opened by this rule.
researchNotes.locator: What is recreational hand panning?; Where can I hand pan?

researchNotes.title: Seasonal guidance
researchNotes.text: The province warns against spring freshet, early-summer high water and significant rain; check wildfire closures and road conditions before travelling.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Use the official panning-reserve maps and current mineral-title information to investigate a specific site; a reserve listing does not waive other restrictions.

statistics.qualifier: Approximate brochure total; do not combine with annual figures.
Separate from lode output; not a current reserve estimate.
Preliminary; includes industrial production, not recreational returns.

overview.text: Yukon placers include high terraces, unglaciated valley fills, interglacial deposits, glacially reworked material and recent alluvium; glacial history changes where older gravels survive.

researchNotes.title: Discovery & mining history
researchNotes.text: The 1896 Bonanza Creek discovery triggered the Klondike rush. Parks Canada credits Keish / Skookum Jim Mason and identifies Káa Goox / Dawson Charlie, Shaaw Tláa / Kate and George Carmack in the discovery party.

researchNotes.title: Rocks & minerals
researchNotes.text: A historical Sulphur Creek operation record describes gold attached to quartz and schist-rich gravels; these are local observations, not universal Yukon indicators.
researchNotes.locator: PDF p. 4, Gold Comments and Surficial Geology

researchNotes.title: Gold geology
researchNotes.text: Sulphur Creek records describe both fine gold and small nuggets, with differences among cuts and years. This historical industrial example cannot predict a visitor’s pan.

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: Annual mine gold production: 6 tonnes; 2024. Preliminary; not separated here into lode and placer.

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: Recreational panning is limited to a pan and shovel on public land that is neither withdrawn nor staked. Ask the Mining Recorder where it is permitted; historic objects, fossils and bones must be left and reported as directed.
researchNotes.locator: Where you can pan; What you can use; historical objects

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: The survey overview organizes ten historical placer regions, including Klondike, Indian River, Mayo, Kluane and Livingstone, to guide further district research.

statistics.qualifier: Preliminary; not separated here into lode and placer.

overview.text: Placer gold is documented in river gravels; the AGS atlas describes Recent and Pleistocene placer occurrences in the western sedimentary basin.

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: AGS describes Alberta gold recovery as a by-product of sand and gravel processing, alongside historical alluvial recovery. This does not measure a hobbyist’s likely recovery.

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: Hand-held nonmechanized recreational panning needs no mineral agreement or licence. A sluicebox or other mechanized placer equipment requires a placer minerals licence. River and stream dredging is prohibited; occupied-land crossings require permission.
researchNotes.locator: Activities — Find out when and where; Sluice for gold

researchNotes.title: Seasonal guidance
researchNotes.text: The toolkit specifies May 15–September 15 for placer operations on Class A/B waters and year-round operations on Class C/D waters, subject to restrictions. This is an operating rule, not a blanket hand-panning season or a safety forecast.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: The toolkit links mineral dispositions, classified water-body maps and Alberta River Basins advisories for site-specific planning.

researchNotes.title: Gold geology
researchNotes.text: In Edmonton’s North Saskatchewan River valley, the museum describes flour-gold flakes often less than half a millimetre across. This locality-specific description is not a measured average for every Alberta river.

researchNotes.title: Rocks & minerals
researchNotes.text: The museum reports platinum flakes with North Saskatchewan River placer gold in smaller amounts. This association is local evidence, not a promise that every black-sand concentrate contains precious metals.

researchNotes.title: Discovery & mining history
researchNotes.text: James Hector reported North Saskatchewan River gold in 1859 after being shown samples from near Fort Edmonton. The museum describes a later dredging boom and the subsequent decline as miners headed to the Klondike.

overview.text: The provincial fact sheet identifies fault-hosted orogenic gold in the Canadian Shield and gold associated with Flin Flon–Creighton volcanogenic massive-sulphide deposits.

researchNotes.title: Gold geology
researchNotes.text: The AGS basin atlas documents Recent and Pleistocene placer gravels in Saskatchewan, alongside Alberta and the Northwest Territories; it says the bedrock sources of these particular placers were unknown.

researchNotes.title: Rocks & minerals
researchNotes.text: At Seabee, shear-hosted quartz-tourmaline veins and biotite alteration accompany gold mineralization; the deposit record lists pyrite and pyrrhotite among host minerals. This is a bedrock example.

researchNotes.title: Discovery & mining history
researchNotes.text: The dated deposit history records Seabee operation production beginning in 1991. The original Seabee deposit and the wider operation using Santoy ore must be distinguished.

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: Recreational testing is pan-only: no shovel, classifier, screen or sluice. Obtain surface-owner permission and authorization for third-party mineral rights. Other equipment needs a claim and applicable approvals; do not damage the bed, bank or boundary of a waterbody.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Use Saskatchewan’s deposit database for geology, dated histories and underlying assessment references; deposit coordinates do not confer collecting permission.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Check MARS tenure and the province’s panning instructions before choosing land or equipment.

overview.text: Timmins gold occurs in ancient volcanic and sedimentary Shield rocks, with gold-bearing quartz veins related to the Porcupine–Destor fault system; glacial deposits cover much of the bedrock.

researchNotes.title: Rocks & minerals
researchNotes.text: Quartz veins are an important Timmins ore setting, but quartz alone is not proof of gold and a bedrock ore photograph is not a typical placer sample.

researchNotes.title: Discovery & mining history
researchNotes.text: The GeoTour describes the 1909 Big Dome discovery by Harry Preston and Jack Wilson, followed by major Hollinger and McIntyre developments.

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: Gold output reported for more than 50 Timmins mines: 70,000,000 ounces; century following 1909. Historical camp figure, not an Ontario total or a precisely dated current cumulative total.

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: Annual mine gold production: 79.9 tonnes; 2024. Preliminary; not a measure of recreational placer opportunity.

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: Ontario’s hobby policy describes conditional enforcement discretion for small personal collections with hand tools, including pans. It is not a blanket exemption. Check mining and surface rights, consent, withdrawals and protected areas; other laws still apply.
researchNotes.locator: PDF pp. 3–6, scope, thresholds, land categories and conditions

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Use the policy’s MLAS and land-status resources before collecting; a mineral occurrence does not establish a right to enter.

statistics.definition: Gold output reported for more than 50 Timmins mines
statistics.qualifier: Rounded historical camp figure, not an Ontario total or a precisely dated current cumulative total.
Preliminary; not a measure of recreational placer opportunity.

overview.text: The Amos bulletin documents Abitibi orogenic quartz-carbonate gold veins in the Bartec and Carpentier zones, plus distinct intrusion-associated styles. This regional example is not a model for every Québec gold occurrence.
overview.locator: Economic Geology — Bartec and Carpentier prospective zones

researchNotes.title: Rocks & minerals
researchNotes.text: Quartz-carbonate gangue and sheared volcanic or intrusive rocks help describe some Amos-area gold settings; these associations require local mapping and sampling, not visual assumptions.

researchNotes.title: Gold geology
researchNotes.text: Val-d’Or–Senneterre Quaternary mapping documents substantial surficial cover. Glacial sediments and transported stones must be considered separately from underlying bedrock.

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: Annual mine gold production: 55.5 tonnes; 2024. Preliminary; not a placer or cumulative historical total.

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: The official guidance distinguishes very superficial prospection from work requiring a DEE, the exclusive exploration right formerly called a claim. Its no-permit wording for limited prospection must not be treated as permission to disturb streambeds or enter any property.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Géologie Québec bulletins link mapped outcrops, analyses and SIGEOM mineralized-site records; use their original scales and regional coverage.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: GESTIM is the official tenure resource identified by the DEE guidance. Verify current title and access conditions before planning fieldwork.

statistics.qualifier: Preliminary; not a placer or cumulative historical total.

overview.text: The Nopiming guide describes Rice Lake gold in Canadian Shield bedrock, unlike the image of easily panned Klondike-style placers; quartz veins hosted historical mines.
overview.locator: PDF pp. 6–7, gold rush and Central Manitoba Mine

researchNotes.title: Rocks & minerals
researchNotes.text: The Central Manitoba Mine worked gold-bearing quartz veins. This is a geological history example, not proof that loose quartz or nearby gravel contains gold.

researchNotes.title: Discovery & mining history
researchNotes.text: In 1911 Duncan Twohearts brought gold-bearing Rice Lake rock to Arthur Quesnel and Captain Pelletier, helping initiate the local rush. The guide’s park context does not authorize collecting.
researchNotes.locator: PDF p. 6, Rice Lake gold discovery

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: The Mines and Minerals Act establishes licensing and open-Crown-mineral-land conditions, subject to surface rights and restrictions. No general recreational-panning waiver was verified in this review; obtain a site-specific answer before collecting.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Begin with the current Mines and Minerals Act and provincial mining administration for title, land-status and consent checks.

researchNotes.title: Rocks & minerals
researchNotes.text: Diana–Gem Lake’s historical inventory describes gold-bearing quartz with arsenopyrite, pyrite, galena and chalcopyrite in an Archean volcanic/intrusive setting. This is deposit-specific ore mineralogy.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Scott Anderson’s Rice Lake project page links structural studies, a field guide and detailed geological maps, including 1:5,000 and 1:10,000 mapping. These explain ore controls rather than recreational permissions.

overview.text: Meguma gold occurs in quartz veins, disseminated metasedimentary rocks and mixed styles within folded Goldenville and Halifax rocks. It is primarily a bedrock-deposit story.

researchNotes.title: Rocks & minerals
researchNotes.text: Quartz, carbonate and sulphides including pyrite, pyrrhotite and arsenopyrite occur in Meguma gold settings. These minerals are not permission to sample old workings.

researchNotes.title: Gold geology
researchNotes.text: The circular describes gold from microscopic grains to coarse specimens across different ore styles. Those ore observations must not become a typical stream-gold size range.

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: Approximate historical gold production: 1,200,000 ounces; 1861–mid-1940s. Approximately 37 tonnes in the source; excludes later production and is not an all-time provincial total.

researchNotes.title: Discovery & mining history
researchNotes.text: Nova Scotia Archives describes the 1858 Mooseland discovery by Captain L’Estrange with Mi’kmaq guide Joe Paul, followed by Paul and John G. Pulsifer’s return and reporting in 1860.
researchNotes.locator: The Gold Rush Years, opening paragraphs

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: Prospector Registration covers preliminary non-ground-disturbing work on open unlicensed ground with landowner permission. Surface disruption requires at least a Mineral Exploration Licence and potentially further approvals. This is not blanket recreational-panning permission.

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: Historic gold tailings may contain arsenic and mercury. The province advises against recreational use of tailings; absence from a mapped inventory is not evidence of safety.
researchNotes.locator: Advice to the public and tailings locations

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Use the registration guidance and its NovaRoc references for current licensing and tenure research.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Information Circular 51 provides a short geological introduction; the 2005 Parsons and coauthors abstract documents historical production and tailings investigations.
researchNotes.locator: IC 51; companion research citation in source catalog

statistics.qualifier: Approximately 37 tonnes in the source; excludes later production and is not an all-time provincial total.

overview.text: The provincial profile documents orogenic, intrusion-related, VMS, skarn, porphyry and epithermal gold, as well as placer and paleoplacer occurrences.

researchNotes.title: Rocks & minerals
researchNotes.text: Cape Spencer includes microscopic gold associated with pyrite; some other deposits involve quartz-carbonate veins and arsenopyrite. Ore mineralogy differs by deposit.

researchNotes.title: Gold geology
researchNotes.text: The profile reports historic panned flakes up to 5 mm in named southwestern rivers, citing Hay (1968). This is a reported maximum from specific occurrences, not a typical size or present recovery promise.

researchNotes.title: Discovery & mining history
researchNotes.text: Cape Spencer became the province’s first primary gold producer in 1986, according to the 2011 profile; this is distinct from earlier by-product production.

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: Approximate historical primary gold output: 150,000 grams; 1986–1988. Mine-specific figure, not provincial total.

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: Prospector licensing and NB e-CLAIMS govern mineral tenure. Mineral rights and surface access are separate; private-land procedures, existing claims and protected or withdrawn lands must be checked. A claim does not remove other approvals.
researchNotes.locator: Licensing, surface access and excluded lands

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: The geological survey links bedrock and surficial maps, a Mineral Occurrence Database and sediment/geochemical survey indexes. Sampling anomalies are exploration evidence, not legal access or guaranteed gold.
researchNotes.locator: Bedrock mapping; Geochemistry; Metallic mineral resources

overview.text: The provincial prospecting article describes gold in quartz veins and gold concealed in sulphides; altered and faulted rocks and stream-sediment sampling can support exploration.
overview.locator: Where to Look; What to Look For

researchNotes.title: Rocks & minerals
researchNotes.text: Quartz and pyrite can occur in gold-bearing settings, but assays may be needed to establish gold that is not visible. Rust or pyrite alone does not identify a gold deposit.

researchNotes.title: Discovery & mining history
researchNotes.text: The article gives historical Baie Verte examples including Goldenville near Ming’s Bight and later Nugget Pond and Hammerdown operations. Its undated present-tense mine claims are excluded.
researchNotes.locator: Where to Look, Baie Verte history

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: The consolidated Mineral Act requires relevant consents for existing mineral titles, private interests and certain government lands. No blanket licence-free stream-panning permission was established here; check tenure, surface rights and water approvals.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: The Matty Mitchell prospecting material supplies a regional introduction and observational checklist; treat its mine-status descriptions as historical until independently updated.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: The geological-survey maps page links bedrock, surficial, geochemical and geophysical maps, with separate simplified geology and prospecting-environment products for Newfoundland and Labrador.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Atlas documentation describes mineral occurrences, bedrock and surficial geology, geochemical surveys, mineral tenure and Labrador Inuit land layers. Geological layers can be downloaded; their presence is not a land-entry decision.
researchNotes.locator: Overview; Land Use; Mineral Lands; Bedrock Geology

overview.text: The Yellowknife greenstone belt hosts major shear-related bedrock gold deposits exemplified by Con and Giant. Industrial lode output does not establish accessible placer gravels.
overview.locator: PDF p. 20, Yellowknife gold exploration context

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: Historical gold production lower bound: 6,000,000 ounces; 1938–2003. Source says more than six million; lower bound, not exact output.

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: Historical gold production lower bound: 7,000,000 ounces; 1948–2004. Source says more than seven million; do not label this an NWT total.

researchNotes.title: Discovery & mining history
researchNotes.text: Con and Giant anchor Yellowknife’s historical gold-mining story; the documented operating periods are 1938–2003 and 1948–2004 respectively.

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: The survey describes a Licence to Prospect before claiming, then a possible mineral lease. The Mining Recorder administers mineral rights and records. This sequence does not itself determine hobby-panning permissions or surface entry.
researchNotes.locator: Exploration Authorization Process; Mining Recorder’s Office

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Consult the Mining Recorder, the linked mineral-tenure viewer and annual NTGS exploration reports; land and water authorizations require separate examination.
researchNotes.locator: Mining Recorder’s Office and linked resources

statistics.qualifier: Source says more than six million; lower bound, not exact output.
Source says more than seven million; do not label this an NWT total.

overview.text: At Portage, Meadowbank, gold occurs principally in banded iron formation, with additional quartz-vein mineralization in metamorphosed volcaniclastic rocks. This is a specific bedrock model.

researchNotes.title: Rocks & minerals
researchNotes.text: Portage mineralization involves pyrrhotite and pyrite replacing magnetite in iron formation, and some gold-bearing quartz veins. These relationships do not make every iron-rich rock prospective.
researchNotes.locator: Abstract; ore and associated mineral assemblages

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: Crown-land exploration uses a Licence to Prospect and Nunavut Map Selection. Claims do not convey surface rights; occupied Crown, Inuit-owned and private lands require applicable consent. Land-use, water and planning approvals may also apply.

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: New prospecting permits stopped being issued in January 2021; this does not mean licences to prospect stopped. Existing transitional permits and current licences are different instruments.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Use CIRNAC’s current Crown-land guidance and Nunavut Map Selection; consult the relevant Inuit landowner and review land-use/water/planning requirements separately.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: The downloadable GSC Portage study includes geological mapping and analytical context; it is research data, not a recreational access map.

researchNotes.title: Discovery & mining history
researchNotes.text: The 2011 overview dates Lupin’s discovery to 1961 and its production to 1982–1998 and 2000–2005. The site lies within present-day Nunavut; much of that history predates the territory’s creation.

researchNotes.title: Production in context
researchNotes.text: The 2011 overview estimates Lupin’s past gold output at 3.37 million ounces over its 1982–2005 operating history, which included shutdowns. This is a mine total spanning the pre-Nunavut administrative period.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Nunavut Geoscience introduces NUMIN occurrence searches and downloadable public assessment reports, Open Files and other geoscience publications. Reported occurrences need source and access checks.

statistics.qualifier: Mine-specific estimate in the 2011 overview, not a Nunavut territory-wide cumulative total; historical boundary change retained.

overview.text: The government water study describes a sandstone-bedrock landscape and erosion-sensitive surface waters. It does not document a gold deposit.

researchNotes.title: Before you prospect
researchNotes.text: The Mineral Resources Act provides a licensing framework subject to landowner rights. No general recreational-gold-panning exemption or approved public panning location was verified in this review.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: The surface-water study is useful for landscape and water context, but must not be presented as a gold-occurrence map.

researchNotes.title: Research tools
researchNotes.text: Use the current consolidated Mineral Resources Act and contact provincial authorities about any proposed mineral collection and land access.
